prerequisites: Foundational knowledge of Materials Science and Technology, Inorganic Chemistry, General Physics, and Mathematical Analysis.

Solid foundation in General Chemistry (atomic structure, chemical bonding, reactivity, and solutions), General Physics (classical mechanics and electromagnetism), and Mathematical Analysis (differential and integral calculus).

learning_outcomes.text: Understand the fundamental working principles of the main microstructural, chemical, physical, and morphological characterization techniques presented during the course.
Select and apply the appropriate analytical techniques for studying and identifying materials, evaluating their advantages, limitations, and complementarities.
Critically process and interpret experimental data and analytical "clues" collected from different instruments.

Synthesize and effectively present the findings of the analytical investigation through a collaborative group presentation (PPT), using appropriate technical terminology and demonstrating effective teamwork.

Possess a solid understanding of the fundamental principles of Materials Science and Technology and Applied Chemistry, comprehending the relationships between atomic structure, defects, diffusion, phase diagrams, and the mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties of the main engineering material classes.

Apply these concepts to evaluate manufacturing processes and heat treatments suitable for optimizing component performance, defining the necessary testing and quality control procedures to ensure compliance with design specifications.
Master basic concepts of water chemistry, including contaminants and treatment methods, as well as the production technology and performance of inorganic binders.

Develop the critical judgment required to select appropriate materials and mitigate degradation phenomena in industrial environments, communicating effectively using proper technical language and demonstrating independence in consulting advanced technical literature and engineering standards.

syllabus_topics: Fundamentals of Spectroscopy & X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF): Spectroscopic notation of electronic transitions. Photoelectric effect and operating principles of XRF instrumentation. X-ray fluorescence yield. Qualitative and quantitative analysis.

X-Ray Diffraction (XRD): Bragg-Brentano geometry. Diffraction patterns of polycrystalline materials; qualitative identification of phase composition, structural and microstructural information. Sample preparation, data acquisition, and phase identification using international databases.

Direct Imaging Techniques (Microscopy & Microanalysis): Fundamentals of optical microscopy. Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): sources, magnetic lenses, and operating principles. Electron-matter interaction: secondary electrons, backscattered electrons, and characteristic X-ray emission (EDS). Sample preparation and morphological/chemical observation via SEM.

Small-Group Laboratory Hands-On Activities: Assignment of unknown material samples to small student teams (max 10 students), guided instrumental observation and data acquisition, processing of raw analytical data, and identification of key analytical clues for material characterization
Module 1: Materials Science and Technology (9 ECTS / 90 hours)

Atomic Structure, Defects, and Solid-State Diffusion: Review of atomic bonding, crystalline and amorphous structures. Crystallography (unit cells, Miller indices, Bravais lattices, interstitial sites) and allotropy. Crystal structures of metals, ceramics, and polymers. Lattice defects (point, line/dislocations and Schmid's law, surface, volume). Solid-state diffusion, Fick's laws, and activation energy.

Mechanical Properties and Testing: Stress and strain concepts. Tensile, compressive, flexural, and hardness tests (Brinell, Rockwell, Vickers, Knoop). Impact testing and ductile-to-brittle transition. Fracture mechanics, fracture toughness, fatigue, and creep behavior.

Phase Diagrams and Phase Transformations: Solid solutions. Binary equilibrium phase diagrams (eutectic, eutectoid, peritectic). Fe-Fe3C phase diagram. Nucleation and grain growth. Transformation kinetics, TTT/CCT diagrams, and martensitic transformations.

Heat Treatments and Strengthening Mechanisms: Solid solution strengthening and strain hardening. Conventional heat treatments of steels (annealing, normalizing, quenching, tempering, hardening, isothermal and surface treatments). Precipitation hardening and aging.

Engineering Alloys and Processing Technologies: Foundry processes, hot/cold plastic deformation, welding, and powder metallurgy. Designation, properties, and applications of ferrous (carbon, alloy, stainless steels, cast irons) and non-ferrous alloys (Al, Mg, Cu, Ni alloys).

Ceramic and Polymeric Materials: Traditional and advanced ceramics, glasses, glass-ceramics, refractories, and processing methods. Thermoplastics, thermosets, and elastomers: polymerization, structure, glass transition temperature (Tg), properties, and processing.

Physical Properties of Materials: Electrical properties (band theory, semiconductors, dielectrics). Thermal properties (heat capacity, thermal expansion, conductivity). Magnetic properties (diamagnetism, paramagnetism, ferromagnetism, soft/hard magnetic materials) and introduction to superconductivity.

Water Chemistry and Treatment Technologies: Physicochemical properties of water, hydrologic cycle, and natural waters. Water hardness. Organic and inorganic contaminants. Water purification, softening, demineralization, and industrial water conditioning.

Inorganic Binders Technology: Definition and classification of binders. Aerial binders (gypsum, aerial lime) and hydraulic binders (hydraulic lime, Portland cement, blended cements). Setting and hardening reactions, microstructure of hydrated cement paste, and concrete durability.
teaching_methods: Classroom Lectures: Introductory theoretical presentation of the working principles behind material characterization techniques (XRF, XRD, SEM/EDS).

Laboratory Practice & Case Studies: Hands-on experiences in small groups (up to 10 students) involving guided observation of analytical instrumentation, sample preparation, and experimental data collection.
Cooperative Teamwork: Group-based data analysis and problem solving to interpret analytical clues, identify unknown samples, and prepare the final team project presentation.
Lectures: Comprehensive presentation of theoretical concepts in Materials Science, Technology, and Applied Chemistry, supported by multimedia slides and board demonstrations.
Guided Classroom Exercises: Resolution of numerical and conceptual problems regarding crystallography, binary phase diagram interpretation, mechanical properties, and water chemistry calculations.

Case Studies and Practical Examples: Guided discussions of real-world examples of material failure, degradation, or selection, aimed at contextualizing fundamental theoretical principles within engineering applications and supporting the learning and understanding of core concepts.

Industrial Field Trips: Guided visits to industrial facilities (such as cement plants or water treatment sites) to observe large-scale manufacturing processes of inorganic binders and industrial water systems firsthand.

assessment_methods.method: Group oral examination (presentation and discussion of slide deck/report on experimental lab activity)

assessment_rules: Student assessment for Complementary Science and Technology of Materials consists of a group oral examination based on the presentation and discussion of a slide deck and/or a concise group report. The final grade reflects preparation levels from Sufficient (18–20/30) to Outstanding (27–30 cum laude). Student learning for Materials Science and Technology is evaluated through an individual oral examination, assessing theoretical knowledge and understanding, ability to link structure, properties, and processing, and use of proper engineering terminology. The final grade will reflect preparation levels from Sufficient (18–20/30) to Outstanding (27–30 cum laude).
